rationale: B wins because it keeps its foot on the evidence brake. Its line "the facts only say none is mentioned — do not assert the absence" is exactly the kind of guardrail that keeps a founder out of a reporter's follow-up trap; A has sharper theater, but "every software company that successfully expands its addressable market deploys sales headcount and a demand-gen machine" is an overconfident universal begging to be disproved. A is useful raw material; B is safer strategic material.
gaps_in_A: "every software company that successfully expands its addressable market deploys sales headcount and a demand-gen machine" — unsupported universal claim. One counterexample and the contrarian angle starts bleeding.

"Productboard, Aha!, and Jira's PM-facing workflows — tools that have long drawn complaints about bloat, slowness, and over-complexity" — plausible category color, but not in the supplied facts. It needs sourcing, not vibes.
"The interface-philosophy question will surface in design and PM community forums within days" — fake predictive peg. Do not invent the reaction before the market has one.
"Pick an angle, then go to `meanest-editor`" — wrong next move for a founder. The next move is proof: customer, pricing, feature specifics, and on-record GTM posture.
gaps_in_B: "taking on the product-management stack" — serviceable, but still a little baggy. Name the subcategory more tightly: roadmapping, stakeholder visibility, PM workflow, not the whole stack.
"Linear bets product managers want a tool that feels built for engineers" — good tension, slightly over-declared. The facts support a question about fit; they do not prove PMs want it.
"journalist-fit-check" as the next step is close, but slightly premature unless the founder can produce the proof B itself demands: pricing, a named team, and on-record no-sales confirmation.
